The attack failed on every axis, and I replaced the verifier's weakest link. The verifier's only witness was the Wikipedia article, which is a fame signal and not a text. I went and got the translation itself.

THE TEXT. publicism.info hosts Richard Bowring's Penguin Classics volume, preface, note on names and dates, the cultural background essay, the full introduction, the translation, and Bowring's own notes, which is why I trust it as the Bowring setting rather than a loose web transcription: the apparatus is his. I downloaded the page (304,739 bytes) and read the joint of the introduction and the text. It runs: the introduction closes on Murasaki's remark about remembering and forgetting, then the head THE DIARY OF LADY MURASAKI, then the first paragraph, which I quote from the file: 'As autumn advances, the Tsuchimikado mansion looks unutterably beautiful. Every branch on every tree by the lake and each tuft of grass on the banks of the stream takes on its own particular colour, which is then intensified by the evening light. The voices in ceaseless recitation of sutras are all the more impressive as they continue throughout the night; in the slowly cooling breeze it is difficult to distinguish them from the endless murmur of the stream.' The proposed sentence is the first sentence of the diary, character for character, comma included, and the locator 'the opening sentence' is exactly right. Note that the file spells it colour, British, which is the Penguin setting and another small sign this is Bowring's own text rather than an Americanised reprint.

TRANSLATION DRIFT, WHICH IS THIS TRACK'S USUAL KILLER, AND WHY IT DOES NOT BITE HERE. The rival English Murasaki diary is Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan (1920), whose opening is wholly different in register and does not produce this wording; anyone who tried to pass Omori and Doi off as Bowring would be caught in the first clause. 'Unutterably beautiful' is Bowring's phrase and is what the line is known by. Bowring's 1982 Princeton edition, Murasaki Shikibu: Her Diary and Poetic Memoirs, is the parent of the 1996 Penguin, and the source line names 1996, which is the published translation this wording comes from, so the naming rule is satisfied and the reader can find the book.

EVERY OTHER GATE. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], murasaki shikibu 0 of 3, not banned. Attribution is not in dispute and is on no trap in the misattribution list. No speaker to name: the diarist is speaking in her own voice. Scope: written about 1008 to 1010, Bowring's translation 1996, both before 1999, not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory. Publishable: a house and a lake in autumn light, nothing needing a warning. Theme fit for Impermanence is the strongest of the four: the mono no aware line at the head of the greatest court diary, beauty seen because the season is turning, and it does the month's work at six in the morning without a word about death. Source line is 97 characters, leads with the author's name, no dash anywhere, and runs work, then locator, then translation with translator and year in parentheses, which is rule 5's order. Tag Diary is the form of the work. The quotation ends in a full stop, carries no quotation marks and no apostrophes, so the curly-quote rule has nothing to catch.

TWO SMALL THINGS FOR THE EDITOR, NEITHER A REFUTATION. First, this is the third or fourth Heian woman in the year: sei shonagon, izumi shikibu and sarashina are each already at 1. Murasaki Shikibu is a distinct person and breaks no cap, but the month's country balance, at most 10 from one country, is where the pressure will show, and August already wants Issa on the carry. Second, the note field is empty. Nothing in the citation needed correcting, so that is defensible, but a one-clause note saying the wording was checked against the Bowring setting would let the next reader see that the opening-sentence claim was tested rather than assumed.
